source.title: TensorCast: The Missing Tensor Management Layer in Large Language Model Infrastructure
source.summary: Modern LLM infrastructure increasingly manages tensors not only as computation data, but also as persistent states shared across distributed components. Existing systems optimize individual tensor management tasks, such as model weight loading, KV cache management, and checkpoint synchronization, by deeply integrating task-specific mechanisms with execution engines, networks, or storage backends. However, this specialization creates isolated silos that hinder the reuse and composition of tensor management strategies across evolving LLM workloads. In this paper, we identify tensor lifecycle management as a missing abstraction layer in LLM infrastructure and propose Tensor-as-a-Service (TaaS), which decouples tensor state management from computation logic. We design and build TensorCast, a distributed tensor management layer that provides first-class tensor abstractions, programmable lifecycle primitives, and a runtime that separates tensor management policies from execution mechanisms. This enables developers to write tensor management programs using TensorCast APIs while transparently leveraging distributed execution and data movement. We integrate TensorCast with vLLM and SGLang and evaluate it across diverse tensor lifecycle workloads, including model weight materialization, weight synchronization, KV cache management, and programmable request routing. Our results show that TensorCast achieves competitive performance with specialized tensor management systems while enabling new cross-component optimization policies. A programmable policy implemented with TensorCast improves median TTFT by up to 93.2% under highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads.

previous_facts.title: TensorCast: The Missing Tensor Management Layer in Large Language Model Infrastructure
previous_facts.event_hint: TensorCast: a distributed tensor-management layer (Tensor-as-a-Service) that decouples tensor lifecycle management from computation, integrated with vLLM and SGLang; a programmable routing policy improves median TTFT by up to 93.2% under highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads.
previous_facts.problem: LLM infrastructure increasingly manages tensors (model weights, KV caches, checkpoints) as persistent distributed states, but existing systems optimize each task (weight loading, KV management, checkpoint sync) by deeply coupling task-specific mechanisms with execution engines, networks, or storage. This creates isolated silos that prevent reuse and cross-component composition, so operators repeatedly reimplement similar lifecycle logic and cannot express optimizations that span multiple components (e.g., jointly balancing load and preserving KV locality).
previous_facts.mechanism: TensorCast proposes Tensor-as-a-Service (TaaS), decoupling tensor state management from computation. It provides first-class tensor abstractions, programmable lifecycle primitives (identify/place/materialize/transform/coordinate), and a runtime that separates tensor-management policies from execution mechanisms. Developers compose tensor-management programs via TensorCast APIs while transparently leveraging distributed execution and data movement; engine-specific state export/import is confined to an instance adaptor so callers evolve without modifying engines, transports, or storage.

evidence.claim: A programmable request-routing policy implemented with TensorCast improves median TTFT by up to 93.2% under highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads.

For high-cardinality KV management (Qwen3-32B, TP=2) with RDMA enabled, TensorCast achieves TTFT reductions of 60% to 87.5% (2.5x to 8x speedup), comparable to the state-of-the-art Mooncake KV backend; with RDMA disabled it significantly outperforms Mooncake.
evidence.baseline: Mooncake KV storage backend in SGLang
evidence.condition: Qwen3-32B TP=2, LongBench prompts (~16k/35k tokens), 100% cache-hit stress test

evidence.claim: TensorCast accelerates model weight synchronization by 1.14x to 2.63x compared with the default updater, evaluated on Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with the WeightPublisher helper publishing versioned weights that rollout workers retrieve per TP-rank slice.
evidence.baseline: Default SGLang updater (full weights from JFS)
evidence.condition: Two-node cluster, 4xH800 per node, RDMA disabled for fairness

evidence.claim: For the programmable router evaluation, three agentic workload presets are defined by inter-turn delay: fast (median 8.2 s), medium (median 20.1 s), slow (median 60.3 s); TensorCast's router shows the smallest cache-hit-rate drop as sessions scale, reducing request TTFT.
evidence.value: fast 8.2 s / medium 20.1 s / slow 60.3 s median inter-turn delay
evidence.condition: Agentic coding workloads, varying session number

evidence.claim: At Qwen3-235B-A22B (TP=8) TensorCast is again comparable to Mooncake under RDMA and better without; TP=8 introduces 4x more concurrent KV-page retrieval requests than TP=2, increasing contention and reducing TTFT improvements for both systems.
evidence.value: comparable (RDMA) / better (no RDMA) than Mooncake at TP=8

previous_facts.evaluation_context: Integrated with vLLM and SGLang. KV-management cluster (Section 6.3): N nodes, each 64 CPU, 1 TB DRAM, 8xH800 GPUs, 200 Gbps RDMA; LongBench prompts grouped ~16k and ~35k tokens; KV reuse stress test forces N-1 instances to concurrently retrieve KV pages (100% cache hit). Weight-sync cluster (Section 6.2): two nodes, 64 CPU, 500 GB DRAM, 4xH800. Models: Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-235B-A22B. Baselines: Mooncake (SGLang HiCache KV backend), default JFS weight updater, and load-aware / cache-aware request routers.
previous_facts.limitations: The authors do not claim a general abstraction is inherently faster than every specialized implementation; TensorCast confines engine coupling to an instance adaptor (integration cost remains). Training-framework integration (Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed) is left to future work. The 93.2% median-TTFT headline is stated as an upper bound under highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads; the exact preset/session-count condition producing that peak is not pinpointable from the reviewed figures. Without RDMA, gains come from a userspace mTCP implementation whose benefit is network-dependent.
previous_facts.project_relevance: Directly relevant to state-aware network / KV-cache scheduling. TensorCast's value-add over pure per-GPU memory scheduling is precisely cross-component composition: a programmable router that jointly balances instance load and KV-cache placement (migrating requests with their KV caches) preserves cache locality and cuts TTFT, and a unified tensor abstraction makes KV transfer, weight sync, and checkpoint resharding reusable rather than siloed. This is concrete evidence for network/coordination-side value beyond GPU-memory scheduling.
source_notes: The 93.2% headline is from the Abstract (PDF Page 1); the router comparison is in Section 6.4 with Figures 10-11 (PDF Page 14).
KV-management and weight-sync numbers are from Sections 6.2-6.3 (PDF Pages 12-13).
Workload delay presets are from Table 3 (PDF Page 13).
